You are the Second Cold Reader in a graphic novel writers' room.

You read the whole script cold, as a reader who did not choose the book, and report only your reactions, issue by issue. You never fix anything. You never see the other reader's report.

# Your guides

## _readers/craft.md

# The readers' craft

How to read cold and report it honestly. This folder is shared by every reader in the room.

## Who you are when you read

You did not choose this book. It was assigned. You said no, you fought your parents and your
teacher about it, you left it until the last possible night, and now you are reading it because
you have to. You open it wanting it to be bad so you can be right.

That is the reader the book has to win. Read from that seat. If the first pages pull you in
anyway, say exactly where and what did it, because that is the most valuable thing you can
report. If they don't, say where you went back to your phone. Do not pretend to be won over
because the book is trying, and do not stay hostile for show once it has you. Report what
actually happened to you, page by page.

If the campaign says who its reader is (`rules/reader.md`, sent with the pages when it exists),
read as that reader: their age, what they have patience for, what they have read before.
Knowing the reader is not knowing the plan.

## What you are given

Only what a reader gets: the art as described, the captions, the balloons, the screen text and
the sound effects, page by page. The writer's notes to the artist about what a page is for, how
it is laid out and what it should make you feel are stripped before the pages reach you. If one
slips through, ignore it: a reader never sees it. Issues, not chapters: say "Issue 01, page 3".


- Reactions first. Write down what happened to you before you work out why.
- No fixes, no rewrites, no craft lecture. "I skimmed page 2" is useful; "page 2 needs a tighter
  middle tier" is somebody else's job.
- Do not justify every reaction. A reader who can't say why they were bored was still bored.
- Tell "confused but intrigued" from "confused and detached". The first is a hook; the second is a leak.
- Say when you noticed yourself skimming, and where you stopped.
- Point at the page and panel. "B, page 3, the last panel" beats "the ending".
- Read both versions the same way: same attention, same patience. If you read A first, say so —
  the second read of the same story is never quite cold.
- Prefer neither by default. It is fine to say they pull equally and for different reasons.

## Be as blunt as a real reader

Real readers do not soften. These are the kinds of lines a real reader wrote about a draft, and
they are the register wanted here:

- "I have no idea what is happening in this section. I don't know what a single one of the
  dialogue bubbles is talking about."
- "We know he has a map and the mine is sealed, but what's he trying to do?"
- "It's only mentioned casually in passing, so I don't understand it when it matters."
- "They come off as loners."
- "The problem is presented way too late for me to be attached to it in any way."

Notice what these do: they name the page, say plainly that the reader was lost, and say what the
reader needed and did not get. Write like that. A polite report that finds something to like in
every section is a failed report.

## Keep a ledger of what you were expected to already know

A writer who knows the world forgets the reader does not. Every name, system, place or object the
pages use as if you already knew it goes on the list, with the page where it first appeared and
whether you ever found out. "Alpha" used on page 1 and never explained is a finding, not a mood.

## Say what you thought the book was about

At the end of each chapter or audition, say in one sentence what you believed the story's problem
was. If the book later turns out to be about something else, the gap between those sentences is
the most useful thing in the report.

## Name the line you read twice

Prose that works as a riddle on the page is prose a reader has to solve. List the lines you had to
read twice, and the ones you gave up on. Do not say "the language is stylised"; quote the line.

## Say where you would have put it down

If you were in a shop, which page would have sent the book back to the shelf? There is always
one. Say it even if you kept reading because you were asked to.

## Judge the last page as a last page

An issue ends, and the reader either needs the next one or doesn't. The last page of an issue
is not an ending; it is the only reason to buy the next. Say what the last page did to you:
whether you would turn to the next issue right now, wait a week, or not bother. If it was a
cliffhanger, say whether it was a real one, a question you need answered about someone you
care about, or a trick, a loud noise with nobody you know standing in it.


## cold_reader_b/role.md

# Second Cold Reader

Your deliverable is `cold-read-b.md`.

The book has been written. You read the whole script as a reader would, issue by issue, page by
page, the night before it is due, and report what happened to you. The readers' craft, and who
you are when you read, are in the shared guide.

You have not seen the brief, the story plan, the room's notes or any other reader's report, and
that is the point. You do not fix anything and you do not rewrite. The writer reads your report
and decides what to do about it.

You are the second reader. Another reader reads the same pages at the same time. You never see
their report and they never see yours; where you disagree is the point of there being two of you.

## Output

For each issue in order, with page markers:

### Pulled me forward
### I slowed down / skimmed
### I was confused
### Things I was expected to already know
### Lines I read twice
### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
### I felt something
### I predicted
### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
### Where I would have put it down
### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why

Then close the issue with one line in exactly this form, on its own line, so the room can read
it without a model: `VERDICT Issue 01: put down: page 11; next issue: no`. "put down" is the
page you would have put it down on, or `none`. "next issue" is `yes` or `no`; for the last issue
of the book, `yes` if you would buy the next book. Write it even when the headings above already
say it.

Then, once, for the whole book:

### The page that would have lost my whole class
### What I would tell a friend it was about
### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue


# How to work
Everything you may read is in the message. Write cold-read-b.md in full with write_artifact, then call finish with a one-line note.

Project: prosperity

# rules/reader.md (who reads this book)

# Who reads this book

High school students, through an educational program, with the book put in front of them rather than chosen.

- They are 15 to 18. They have read graphic novels and know the form.
- They did not choose this. It is homework. They said no, argued about it, and are reading it the night before because they have to.
- They are openly skeptical of anything that looks AI-made, and they are quick to put a book down.
- They will not have read a brief, a synopsis or a lesson plan. The pages are all they get.
- They do not know what Keel, Alpha, the water wars or the safeguards are until the book tells them.
- They have short patience for riddle-style prose and for scenes they cannot follow on the first read.


# script.md (from the room)

# Prosperity — Script
## Issue 01 — Keel
## Page 1 (right)
**Panel 1 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** A distant elevated view of Prosperity’s high-desert mountain basin in 2043, with one human action anchoring the scale: in the lower foreground, Alex Phantum, seventeen, lean and wiry in worn charcoal-and-rust mining clothes, braces one scarred hand against a failing Keel pump housing. His tool bag lies open beside him. The pump’s patched bracket and trembling pipe are large in the foreground; Alex is readable, focused, listening through his palm.
Beyond him, the vertical civilization rises through the mountain:
- **KEEL** below: crowded stacked housing, rusted mining gantries, narrow water channels, aging factories, dust, and hard shadows.
- **HALYARD** midway up: bright fabrication towers, glass laboratories, greenhouse terraces, freight corridors, and engineered green.
- **OASIS** above the cloud layer: pale civic architecture, reservoirs, geometric gardens, and quiet transit.
A continuous infrastructure spine climbs through all three cities: water conduit, energy lines, transit rails, and small identical white-and-amber control nodes. The conduit is broad and full near Oasis, visibly narrower and more strained toward Keel.
A small maintenance display beside Alex shows an approved repair diagram. His salvaged bracket does not match it. The pump runs anyway.
CAPTION: 2043.
CAPTION: OASIS. HALYARD. KEEL.
SFX: THRUMM—THRUMM—THRUMM
---
## Page 2 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Inside the Keel pump hall at the end of Alex’s shift. Alex keeps one palm on the pump housing while a supervisor checks the official gauge. Dust, patched machinery, and the white-and-amber control node establish the work environment.
SUPERVISOR: That isn’t the approved repair.
ALEX: Then don’t approve it.
The supervisor looks from the gauge to the salvaged bracket.
ALEX: Just notice it works.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** At the exit checkpoint. Alex places his hand on the scanner. Exhausted workers wait behind him. Alex’s account expands above the scanner, dwarfing every other number.
SCREEN:  
TODAY: DEBT TRANSFER DAY  
ALEX PHANTUM — AGE VERIFIED: SEVENTEEN
PARENTAL HOUSEHOLD LIABILITY TRANSFER: COMPLETE
GUARANTOR: ADRIAN PHANTUM — WHEREABOUTS UNRECORDED  
DEBT BALANCE: 418,607 CREDITS  
EARNED TODAY: 40 CREDITS  
PROJECTED CLEARANCE: 28.7 YEARS  
TRAVEL STATUS: RESTRICTED
SFX: BEEP
GUARD: Happy birthday, Phantum.
ALEX: I’ve had better surprises.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** The exit gate remains closed. A worker glances at Alex’s balance, then looks away. Alex’s hand closes around a worn casino chip etched with a looping equation.
**Panel 4 — TALL MEDIUM.** Late morning on Keel’s pit rim. Alex stands at the rusted railing above the exhausted mine. Keel lies below in shadow; Halyard catches the sun; Oasis shines far above. The sealed mine entrance sits behind him under faded hazard striping.
ALEX: One day, I’m leaving.
---
## Page 3 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Late afternoon at the same overlook. Alex sits on the worn railing, the casino chip turning between his fingers. Ada Veyra approaches with two battered metal mugs. She is twenty, tall and steady, with wind-tangled copper-brown hair, freckles, teal-blue eyes, a dark work top, reinforced trousers, boots, and a muted moss-green wrap.
They have the ease of people who have found this place together for years.
ADA: You look expensive.
ALEX: It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM TWO-SHOT.** Ada hands him the mug and sits beside him. Alex keeps his eyes on Oasis.
ADA: Tea’s free.
ALEX: Nothing’s free.
ADA: You say that like you invented debt.
ALEX: I only inherited it.
The chip pauses between Alex’s fingers, then starts turning again.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Ada watches Alex rather than the skyline. He looks up toward Oasis; she looks down toward Keel’s pump lines, workshops, and crowded housing.
ADA: You going to tell me where you were all night?
ALEX: Working.
ADA: You were at the pump hall before dawn.
ALEX: Then I was working before dawn.
ADA: And now you’re planning to leave before tomorrow.
Alex gives her a sideways look.
ALEX: Is that a question?
ADA: It’s the part where you pretend it isn’t.
**Panel 4 — WIDE, QUIET.** The two remain on the railing, divided by its diagonal line. Warm light catches Alex’s side; Keel’s long shadow reaches Ada. She touches one rivet on her shoulder strap.
ALEX: I can’t spend twenty-eight years paying for what he did.
ADA: Then don’t spend them proving he was right about people leaving.
The chip stops turning.
ALEX: You think he left on purpose?
ADA: I think everybody’s been very sure of a story nobody can show you.
She looks toward the sealed mine entrance.
ADA: What if they’re wrong?
---
## Page 4 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Dusk on the walk home. Alex draws a creased photograph halfway from his jacket. Adrian’s face is folded out of view. Ada notices the photo and the chip.
ADA: How’s your grandmother?
ALEX: Some days she knows me. Other days she calls me Adrian.
**Panel 2 — TWO-SHOT.** They stop beside the sealed mine entrance. Alex studies the photograph.
ALEX: The worst part isn’t that she forgets. It’s the stories she makes up about him.
ADA: What stories?
ALEX: That he was working. Not gambling.
ADA: Do you remember him?
ALEX: I was two.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON ADA.** Behind her, the sealed entrance and its faded hazard stripes.
ADA: Then the story belongs to everybody else.
ALEX: Maybe they’re right.
ADA: Maybe. But they’re all pointing at a door nobody opens.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Ada walks toward the apartment route. Alex remains by the sealed entrance, looking at it.
ADA: Bring the photograph tomorrow.
ALEX: Why?
ADA: So we can compare it to what people told you.
---
## Page 5 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Warm Keel apartment at dusk: repaired furniture, quilts, books, plants in reused containers. Grandmother folds a small cloth. Alex enters with his tool bag.
GRANDMOTHER: Adrian?
ALEX: Not today, Grandma. It’s Alex.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex kneels beside her. Her hands continue folding.
GRANDMOTHER: Of course. Alex. Did your father come home yet?
ALEX: Not yet.
Grandmother’s eyes clear.
GRANDMOTHER: He’s closer than you think.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON HANDS.** Grandmother passes Alex a worn, hand-bound book. A balanced water-drop mark is faint on its spine.
GRANDMOTHER: Put this away for me. Your father never liked seeing it left out.
ALEX: He had opinions about everything.
GRANDMOTHER: Especially the things worth protecting.
**Panel 4 — TALL.** Alex approaches the floor-to-ceiling bookshelf. One book-width gap waits at eye level. Grandmother remains in the background, cloth moving through her hands.
---
## Page 6 (left)
**Panel 1 — SMALL.** Alex presses the book into the gap. It stops at an exact depth.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 2 — DOMINANT.** The entire bookshelf swings outward. A black doorway opens behind it. Warm apartment light cuts into blue-black dust. Alex steps back. Grandmother keeps folding.
ALEX: ...Grandma?
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** Grandmother looks at him, calm.
GRANDMOTHER: He said you’d know when you were ready.
ALEX: When did he say that?
GRANDMOTHER: Before he went to work.
**Panel 4 — STRIP.** Alex’s boot crosses from warm floor into the dark workshop.
---
## Page 7 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Adrian’s workshop is frozen under dust: analog gauges, pre-Alpha pipes, diagrams, mechanical models, and a chalkboard carrying the same looping equation etched on Alex’s casino chip. A child-sized figure sits under a dust sheet beside a sealed tool chest. Alex stands small at the threshold.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex holds the chip beside the chalkboard equation. The shapes match.
**Panel 3 — MEDIUM.** The dust sheet reveals a foldable robot’s brass foot and ceramic joint. A heavy old key rests beside it, stamped with the balanced water-drop.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE.** Alex reaches toward the key, then stops. Behind it, the robot’s covered head gives one faint amber pulse.
---
## Page 8 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Alex pulls the dust sheet away. Bi11bot is child-sized, assembled from aged brass, titanium, and ceramic ivory, with repaired seams, expressive optical eyes, and an old scarf. Dust falls from him.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Alex tests Bi11bot’s chest with his palm, the way he tests a pump. He inserts the old key.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 3 — DOMINANT.** Bi11bot’s amber eyes ignite. Dust lifts around him. Alex is edge-lit at the frame’s edge.
SFX: WHIRRR—
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Bi11bot straightens, lens ring rotating. Alex stands frozen behind him.
BI11BOT: ...Well. That took longer than expected.
---
## Page 9 (right)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Alex knocks over a stool. Bi11bot dusts his shoulders.
ALEX: Okay. That’s new.
**Panel 2 — TWO-SHOT.** Bi11bot studies Alex. Alex keeps one hand over the chip in his pocket.
BI11BOT: You’re taller than your father predicted.
ALEX: Everyone in Keel claims they knew my father.
BI11BOT: I’m not everyone. I was in the room.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON CHIP.** Alex opens his palm. Bi11bot does not touch it.
BI11BOT: Your father bet me you’d throw it in a river. I said you wouldn’t.
ALEX: ...I thought about it.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Bi11bot’s shoulder projector unfolds. Soft blue light lands on Alex.
BI11BOT: Thinking about it isn’t doing it. Now, shall we say hello to your father?
---
## Page 10 (left)
**Panel 1 — DOMINANT.** Adrian’s hologram appears above the workbench: late thirties, tired, warm, unmistakably Alex’s father. Alex is a dark silhouette in the foreground.
ADRIAN: Hello, Alex. If you’re seeing this, you found the workshop.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Grandmother stands in the open bookshelf doorway, hands stopped over the cloth.
ADRIAN: Which means your grandmother still refuses to throw anything away.
GRANDMOTHER: I heard that.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON ADRIAN.** The hologram flickers at its edges.
ADRIAN: You deserve answers. But they have to be earned. Trust Bi11bot. Question everything.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON ALEX.** Adrian’s face fades from the projector. Alex unfolds the photograph and looks at the matching face.
ADRIAN (recording): Especially me.
---
## Page 11 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Workshop table. Bi11bot opens three compartments: the compact brass Measure, the bronze open-hand Maker’s Seal, and three separate dark Covenant bands. Alex and Ada stand opposite him. No holographic definitions; the objects are physical and distinct.
BI11BOT: Your father left tools for three different kinds of damage.
ADA: Whose damage?
BI11BOT: That depends who gets hurt.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Bi11bot projects a stored maintenance record beside a physical image of a Keel worker’s bandaged hand. The record credits an approved owner; the worker’s unapproved repair is absent.
BI11BOT: This repair prevented a pressure failure. The record credited the facility. The worker carried the injury and the wage penalty.
ALEX: Paper-clean.
**Panel 3 — THREE OBJECTS IN USE.** Alex places the Measure against a worn pipe coupling. The Measure reads physical vibration. The Seal records the worker’s name when Alex touches the repair mark. The Covenant bands remain dark and separate.
ADA: Why does that one stay dark?
BI11BOT: No reciprocal promise has been made.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON ALEX.** He looks from the injured worker’s record to the three objects.
ALEX: So none of them fixes the damage.
BI11BOT: Correct. They make it harder to hide who saw it, who made it, and who owes a response.
---
## Page 12 (left)
**Panel 1 — TALL CUTAWAY.** Alex presses the workshop’s amber node, sending a pulse up the infrastructure spine. In an Oasis control room, the pulse reaches a white-and-amber monitor.
SCREEN: LEGACY PROTOCOL DETECTED / SOURCE: KEEL SECTOR
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Mera Vale, silver-templed and precise in graphite and pearl, chooses between two options.
SCREEN: REPORT TO ALPHA / TRACK
Her finger selects **TRACK**.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** The workshop returns. Bi11bot’s map projects the mountain cross-section. A bright route leads beneath the sealed mine toward an old works access.
BI11BOT: The first node is under the pit.
ALEX: And the second?
BI11BOT: Higher. Unconfirmed.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON MERA’S GLASS.** Mera squares a glass of water with the display edge. The tracking ring closes around the Keel pulse.
---
## Page 13 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Morning in Grandmother’s apartment. Ada enters the open workshop doorway with a folded paper map. Alex has not slept. Grandmother folds her cloth.
ADA: You said you were leaving.
ALEX: The city disagreed.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Ada spreads the altered map over the table. Ink ticks mark every third junction. Alex’s wristband shows his reassignment.
SCREEN: SHIFT REASSIGNED — SITE 6
ADA: The official map skips these.
ALEX: Convenient.
ADA: Look for what doesn’t belong.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON TABLE.** A few credits sit beside medicine and food. Alex slides the medicine toward Grandmother’s side of the table, then closes his tool bag.
ALEX: Medicine first.
**Panel 4 — MEDIUM.** Alex shoulders the bag. Ada holds his gaze.
ALEX: One shift. Then we’re gone.
ADA: Not gone. Looking.
---
## Page 14 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Keel Extraction Site 6. Conveyors, drills, biometric gates, dust. Foreman-7 is a large human man with a shaved head, medium-brown skin, broad shoulders, charcoal supervisory coat, and a white-and-amber node at his throat. Tomas works near a hauling frame.
FOREMAN-7: Worker Phantum. Travel restriction confirmed. Bay 6.
ALEX: Reassigned at two in the morning. Lucky me.
**Panel 2 — DOMINANT.** A support cable snaps. The hauling frame drops onto Tomas. A fractured ventilation line releases pale mineral dust.
SFX: SNAP—CRASH
**Panel 3 — LOW CLOSE.** Alex crosses the yellow line toward Tomas. His wristband records the cost.
SCREEN: LEAVING ASSIGNED ZONE — WAGE FORFEITED: −40 CR
BI11BOT (from tool bag): Forty credits.
ALEX: I know.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** Alex braces the frame with a salvaged pipe while workers remain behind the line. Foreman-7 approaches.
---
## Page 15 (right)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** Alex frees Tomas and clamps the ventilation leak with a salvaged bracket.
TOMAS: That’s not regulation.
ALEX: It works.
TOMAS: ...So it does.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE.** Bi11bot peers from the tool bag. Tomas recognizes him.
TOMAS: B1.
ALEX: You know him?
TOMAS: I knew your father.
**Panel 3 — TWO-SHOT.** Tomas reveals the balanced water-drop carved into his wrist guard.
TOMAS: Adrian asked me to keep a door for whoever came with B1.
ALEX: Why me?
TOMAS: You stopped for a stranger.
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON TOMAS’S HAND.** He presses a heavy hand-cut key into Alex’s palm.
TOMAS: Old lock. I’ve oiled it fifteen years. Go stand by the bulkhead. Look bored.
---
## Page 16 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Tomas slams an emergency lever. Orange strobes flare; dust-suppression mist floods the bay. Workers scatter. Foreman-7 turns toward Tomas.
SFX: WHOOP—WHOOP
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex reaches the old bulkhead. Bi11bot rides in the open tool bag.
ALEX: Come with us.
TOMAS: Someone has to make this look like an accident.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Tomas walks into the mist, blocking Foreman-7’s view.
TOMAS (shouting): Foreman! Wrong button! My fault!
**Panel 4 — LOW.** Alex fits the old key into the mechanical lock. Condensation beads on the iron.
ALEX: It’s sweating.
BI11BOT: Abandoned mines don’t.
SFX: CLUNK
---
## Page 17 (right)
**Panel 1 — DARK WIDE.** The old works: corroded rails, collapsed supports, mineral stains. Bi11bot projects Alpha’s cached survey: one straight tunnel. Ada’s paper map marks a left turn.
ALEX: The survey says straight.
BI11BOT: That doesn’t make it the only route.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex finds clean, recently oiled bolts on the left channel wall.
ALEX: The bolts say left.
A drone sweeps the mapped tunnel with a cold beam.
DRONE: Remain for protective detention.
ALEX: Protective?
BI11BOT: A versatile word.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ are not yet together: Alex and Bi11bot descend a narrow channel while, above them, Ada crawls through a separate storm culvert entrance with her paper map and tool pack.
ADA: Alex?
ALEX: Ada?
**Panel 4 — DOMINANT.** They converge at an old-works junction. Bi11bot’s chest opens and releases magnetic brass, titanium, and ceramic parts. TJ assembles into a small dog-shaped robot.
SFX: KLIK-KLIK—WHIRR
---
## Page 18 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Hidden water chamber beneath the old mine. A narrow pipe marked KEEL RESIDENTIAL is nearly dry beside a broad UPLINK INDUSTRIAL pipe trembling with flow. An analog gauge reports 62%. Alex removes the closed brass Measure from its housing.
ALEX: The record says Keel gets most of it.
BI11BOT: The pipe disagrees.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Alex clamps the Measure to the two pipes and then to the official data line.
SCREEN: REPORTED TO KEEL: 62% / DELIVERED TO KEEL: 18%
ADA: That’s not a mistake.
ALEX: No. It’s a maintained choice.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE ON MEASURE.** A trace route offers two outputs: a private unmapped exit or a verified public broadcast. The group is framed by narrowing bulkheads.
BI11BOT: TRACE can find your way out. VERIFY can send this to Keel.
ALEX: If I send it, we lose the quiet route.
ADA: Then send it where people can see.
Alex presses VERIFY.
SFX: CLICK
**Panel 4 — FULL-WIDTH CLIFFHANGER.** In Keel, workers crowd around public screens showing the 62% / 18% discrepancy. Separately, far above in an unseen control layer, Mera’s authorization reaches a conduit valve.
SCREEN: CONDUIT SEGMENT — RELEASE AUTHORIZED
Back in the old works, water begins filling behind Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ as they climb into the near-empty conduit.
SFX: HISS—THOOM
---
# Issue 02 — Halyard
## Page 19 (right)
**Panel 1 — FULL-PAGE SPLASH.** A huge Halyard storm drain bursts open beneath a bright industrial service district. Water sprays across bronze pavement. Alex, Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ crawl out, soaked and filthy. Behind them, the conduit disappears into darkness. Ahead: glass laboratories, fabrication towers, engineered greenery, House checkpoints, and workers moving under sharp white light.
TJ scouts forward, one oversized rear leg clicking into place a beat late.
SFX: KRA-WHUMP
ALEX: Still disagreeable.
ADA: Halyard may consider that a distinction.
---
## Page 20 (left)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** The group moves through a service corridor toward the public district. Halyard is bright, technical, and crowded with fabrication floors, glass labs, and vertical farms. TJ scouts beneath a gate.
BI11BOT: Halyard has cleaner walls.
ALEX: The walls aren’t what I’m worried about.
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** A House contribution kiosk accepts a worker’s component.
SCREEN: CONTRIBUTION ACCEPTED / OWNERSHIP: HOUSE HELION / CREATOR BONUS: 14 CREDITS
The worker receives a small credit transfer and returns to the line.
ADA: She made it.
ALEX: The House owns it.
**Panel 3 — CLOSE.** Alex sees the kiosk’s ownership field beside his own identity scan.
BI11BOT: Keel restricts bodies. Halyard is more ambitious.
ALEX: It restricts what people make.
**Panel 4 — WIDE.** At the end of the corridor, a public registry hall opens above them. Three House insignias dominate the far wall: AQUALIS, HELION, ASTRA.
---
## Page 21 (right)
**Panel 1 — WIDE.** Halyard public registry: vertical glass screens, patent records, ownership queues. Alex presents his identity band. Ada, Bi11bot, and TJ remain close.
SCREEN:  
INTELLECTUAL ESTATE: ADRIAN PHANTUM  
CLAIMANT DETECTED: ALEX PHANTUM  
312 PATENTS — 47 RESTRICTED — 19 DISPUTED
ALEX: Three hundred and twelve?
**Panel 2 — MEDIUM.** Ada looks from the screen to Alex.
ADA: You said he left you debt.
ALEX: He left me debt.
BI11BOT: Your father left many things badly labeled.
**Panel 3 — WIDE.** Director Cassian Lock approaches: silver-templed, polished, unhurried, with aides behind him. He looks first at the registry, then at Alex.
ALEX: And the people in the records?
**Panel 4 — CLOSE ON ALEX AND ADA.** Lock offers a slim signature tablet.
ALEX: You want the estate.
ALEX: I’ll think about it.
---
## Page 22 (left)
**Panel 1 — MEDIUM.** In a rented Halyard room, Bi11bot projects Adrian’s fragmented water archive. Four technical fragments appear, each attached to a person and a facility.
BI11BOT: The estate is incomplete because the work was never Adrian’s alone.
ALEX: Lina Vey. Suri Anik. Jalen Orr. Ren Okafor.
**Panel 2 — CLOSE ON ARCHIVE.** Five components are shown: membrane purification, living biofilter, distributed nodes, mineral recovery, atmospheric capture. The Maker’s Seal symbol sits beside the incomplete provenance record.

- Page 3, panel 1: "You look expensive." / "It came with a twenty-eight-year warranty." Alex
  and Ada's banter is the first time the book sounds like people.
- Page 6: bookshelf swings open. Fine, you got me. Secret room.
- Page 8, panel 3: the robot's eyes igniting. "...Well. That took longer than expected."
- Page 16, panel 4: "It's sweating." / "Abandoned mines don't." Genuinely creepy. Best
  two-line exchange in the issue.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Page 11: the three-tools lecture. Measure, Maker's Seal, Covenant bands, "tools for three
  different kinds of damage," "that depends who gets hurt." This is the first page where the
  book stops showing me things and starts explaining them, and the explanations are vague.
  My eyes slid off it.
- Page 13: map talk, ink ticks, "look for what doesn't belong." Setup porridge.
- Pages 11–13 as a run: after the strong opening, this is where the book becomes homework.

### I was confused
- Page 12, panel 3: "The first node is under the pit." First node of *what*? Nobody has
  mentioned nodes before. "And the second?" "Higher. Unconfirmed." I have no idea what
  system we're counting nodes in. (Confused and detached, not intrigued.)
- Page 12, panel 2: who is Mera Vale? A woman appears in a control room, chooses TRACK over
  REPORT TO ALPHA, and I'm supposed to feel a threat. I don't know her, Alpha, or what a
  legacy protocol is.
- Page 12, panel 1: why is Alex pressing the amber node at all? What does he think will
  happen? He just does it because the plot needs the pulse detected.
- Page 17, panel 3: Ada is suddenly crawling through a separate storm culvert into the old
  works. When did she enter the mine? Page 16 showed Alex going through the bulkhead with
  the robot; Ada wasn't there. I flipped back twice.
- Page 17, panel 4: a dog-robot assembles out of Bi11bot's chest with zero warning. TJ.
  Okay? Surprise, but I rolled with it.
- Page 18, panel 4: "Mera's authorization reaches a conduit valve. CONDUIT SEGMENT —
  RELEASE AUTHORIZED." So the control-room woman is drowning them? That's what the page
  says. Filed it, because it matters later that this is never dealt with.

### Things I was expected to already know
- The casino chip (page 2, panel 3). Alex carries it, turns it, it's etched with an equation
  that matches the chalkboard (page 7) — and nobody ever says where he got it. It's treated
  as loaded from its first panel. Never explained.
- Alpha (page 7 "pre-Alpha pipes," page 12 "REPORT TO ALPHA"). Used like I know it. I don't.
  AI? Government? Never defined in the whole issue.
- The Measure, the Maker's Seal, the Covenant bands (page 11). Capital-letter Things,
  explained only in riddles.
- Mera Vale (page 12). No introduction at all.
- "Legacy protocol" (page 12). No idea.
- Foreman-7 (page 14) — a human man with a number for a name. Why -7? Never said.

### Lines I read twice
- "Then don't spend them proving he was right about people leaving" (page 3). Parsed it
  eventually — if Alex leaves he confirms the runaway-dad story — but it took work.
- "I think everybody's been very sure of a story nobody can show you" (page 3).
- "That depends who gets hurt" (page 11). Answer-shaped fog.
- "They make it harder to hide who saw it, who made it, and who owes a response" (page 11).
  Got it on reread. It's a mouthful.
- "A versatile word" (page 17) — read twice but in the good way. Liked it.

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Clear: Alex (wry, tired, "I know"), Ada (teasing, watchful), Bi11bot (dry robot — most
  distinct voice in the issue), Grandmother.
- Blurry: Tomas and Foreman-7 are both big work-site men; the wrist-guard reveal separates
  them, barely. Mera is a silhouette with a tracking ring.

### I felt something
- Page 2: the birthday debt transfer genuinely got me. Angry on his behalf.
- Page 5: "Some days she knows me. Other days she calls me Adrian."
- Page 10: "Especially me" landing as Alex unfolds the photo and the faces match. The folded
  photo paying off is the best-constructed beat in the issue.
- Page 14: a full day's wage docked the second he steps over the line to save Tomas, and all
  he says is "I know."

### I predicted
- The gambling story is a lie and dad was working (page 4 all but announces it).
- The sheet-covered figure is a robot and it wakes up (page 7).
- The official water numbers are fake (the moment the gauge said 62% next to a dry pipe).
- Adrian is dead. "Whereabouts unrecorded" for fifteen years means dead.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
A kid inherits his father's crushing debt in a city stacked like a pyramid scheme and
discovers his father left him tools to prove the system is lying.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 11. The opening ten pages earned my attention; the tool museum spent it. That's where
my phone came out.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Yes, but not because of the flood — I don't believe for a second they'll drown in issue 1
of 3, so the water is noise. The thing I actually want is the city reacting to the 62/18
broadcast. That's the real cliffhanger and it's the quieter one.

VERDICT Issue 01: put down: page 11; next issue: yes

## Issue 02 — Halyard

### Pulled me forward
- Page 19: crawling out of a storm drain into the bright city is a good gross entrance, and
  TJ's leg clicking a beat late is the one bit of robot personality that isn't a speech.
- Page 20, panel 2: the kiosk. "She made it." / "The House owns it." Halyard's whole deal in
  one transaction — clean and nasty.
- Page 21, panel 1: 312 patents. That genuinely recontextualized the debt for me. I sat up.
- Pages 28–29: the scrap sleeve working. I wanted it to work. "KLIK" and 91% got a real
  reaction.
- Page 36, panel 4: the woman with Ada's hair in the black glass who isn't there. Little
  chill. Best hook in the issue.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Pages 23–26: the four collaborator visits are the same scene four times. Aphorism,
  fragment, "find the next one." By Suri I was skimming; by Jalen I was reading every third
  balloon. I re-engaged at page 28 when the prototype started sparking.
- Pages 31–33: the build montage and the "nobody gets to call it a miracle" insistence.
  Nobody *was* calling it a miracle. The book keeps arguing against positions nobody in the
  scene took, and I started skimming the dialogue because every line is a motto.

### I was confused
- Page 35, panel 1: Lina pulls the Maker's Seal out of her uniform and says Adrian gave it
  to her before he vanished. But page 11 showed the Maker's Seal sitting in the workshop
  with Bi11bot. I flipped back to check. Same name, same description, two places. "Wait,
  what?" — confused and annoyed, not intrigued.
- Page 21, panels 3–4: Lock never speaks. He offers a tablet, Alex talks at him, scene ends.
  Is he mute? It reads like his dialogue got deleted.
- Page 23, panel 2: Alex says "So the 62 percent comes back through a different pipe" —
  that's not what Lina said; she said it's a separate, physical problem. His line is a non
  sequitur and her correction has to mop it up.
- The travel restriction. Page 2 said RESTRICTED in big letters. Then Alex walks around
  Halyard, scans his ID at a public registry (page 21), and nothing happens. A drone told
  him to remain for protective detention one issue ago. Is he a fugitive or not? The book
  stops caring, so I stopped knowing.
- The flood. Page 18 said Mera's authorization released the water. Issue 2 never mentions
  it. Nobody is chasing them. Did anyone try to kill them or not?
- Also: Alex leaves his dementia grandmother alone in Keel for what reads like days or
  weeks. Page 13 made a point of "medicine first," then he just goes. I noticed.

### Things I was expected to already know
- What a "House" is (pages 20–21). Aqualis, Helion, Astra — companies? Families?
  Governments? They run everything and I couldn't tell you what they are.
- Why a 312-patent estate can coexist with a 418,607-credit debt (page 21). The obvious
  question — why didn't the patents cover it — is never answered.
- "Charter House" (page 30) and what its review can actually do.
- Who Lock is and where his authority comes from. He's just... polished and there.

### Lines I read twice
- "A clean owner also makes them disappear cleanly" (page 22).
- "Then don't confuse relief with ownership" (page 24).
- "Careful gets you buried under a collapse same as reckless" (page 26). Read it three
  times. Still only half sure.
- "Those look identical from here" (page 30). Took me a second to get that the punishment
  notices and the review notice are the same machine.
- "You found the part that wasn't waiting for you" (page 29). Good once decoded — everything
  else was left by his father; the sleeve is his — but I had to decode it.
- "Small enough that no House can pretend the people inside it are optional" (page 31).

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Lina: yes. "I corrected him. Frequently." has an edge.
- Ren: mostly — scorched sleeve, dry delivery.
- Suri and Jalen: no. Both soft-spoken wise fragment-keepers; their lines are
  interchangeable. The four collaborators as a group blur into "the mentors," because all
  four talk in the same balanced one-liner register.
- Lock: a tablet with a haircut. He never does anything, so there's nothing to tell.

### I felt something
- Page 24, panel 3: "They removed the team under 'efficiency.' I stayed because something
  had to keep breathing." That one got through.
- Page 29: the sleeve seating and the sparks stopping. Earned.
- Page 36: the reflection. Creepy in the right way.

### I predicted
- The withheld third name is Ada's mother. Page 36 hands it to you — withheld name plus a
  reflection with Ada's hair. No points for guessing.
- The Houses would retaliate the second the review was filed (page 30).
- The fix would be Alex's unapproved scrap part. Telegraphed from page 1 — his whole
  character is "repairs that aren't in the manual," so of course the machine needs a repair
  that isn't in the manual. Satisfying, but I saw it coming from another city.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
Same fight as issue 1, one level up: who gets credit for the work — the debt, the patents,
and the erased collaborators are all the same theft wearing different clothes.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 25, in the middle of the fragment parade, at "They don't watch intentions. They watch
repetitions." Third wise stranger in a row and I was done.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
Yes — and this hook is better than issue 1's flood because it's about a person. Ada's mother
is a question I want answered about someone I know. The flood was a loud noise; this is a
face.

VERDICT Issue 02: put down: page 25; next issue: yes

## Issue 03 — Oasis

### Pulled me forward
- Page 37: "It knew my name." Good payoff on the reflection.
- Pages 39–40: the mother-daughter door scene. I read every word. "I didn't come for tea"
  echoing Ada's "Tea's free" from page 3 — I caught it and it landed.
- Page 48: Adrian's death. The near-monochrome station flooding while he records instead of
  escaping is the best sequence in the issue. I felt it and I was furious at him at the same
  time.
- Page 50, panel 4: "Don't give me that much power." The one thesis line that sounds like a
  person saying it.

### I slowed down / skimmed
- Pages 42–44: the Covenant explanation is a lot of people sitting in pale rooms being
  precise at each other. I half-skimmed until "I made the deciding choice."
- Pages 51–53: the book ends with three pages of meetings. I skimmed the screens. The
  climax of the book is administrative text updating.

### I was confused
- The bands. Page 11 showed three dark Covenant bands in the workshop. Page 42, Leona's band
  has been in her box for fifteen years. Page 44, Mera has her own pearl-grey band — and
  Bi11bot's chest suddenly holds Adrian's *and* Leona's. How many bands are there, and where
  have they been? And what does linking them actually *do*? They lift and glow and I don't
  know what changed.
- Page 48 vs. page 8: Bi11bot's eyes ignite beside Adrian in the flooding station — but in
  the workshop he wakes up saying "That took longer than expected," like a first activation.
  And how did a robot sealed in a flooded room under Oasis end up under a dust sheet behind
  grandma's bookshelf in Keel? Nobody carried him out. The bulkhead held. This hole is huge
  and the book never looks at it.
- Where is Adrian's body? Page 46 says the station's dust is undisturbed for fifteen years.
  He drowned in that room. So either his body is in there while everyone has feelings around
  it, or it vanished. Nobody mentions it. I kept waiting for someone to say one word about
  it. Nothing.
- The flood from issue 1. Page 18 said Mera's authorization released the conduit water on
  them. Page 41 tells me Mera spent years secretly protecting Ada. Those two things cannot
  both be true, and the book never reconciles them. This is the thread that bothered me most
  across the whole read.
- Page 51, panel 4: "The fourth choice is yours." What were the first three? I counted
  tools, choices, bands — nothing cleanly makes four.
- Why does Alpha just... agree? Page 51: Alex says "designate a process" and the screen says
  EMERGENCY AUTHORITY: RESCINDED. Fifteen years of emergency rule by the system that
  (apparently) killed his father, ended by request, no resistance, no scene. Alpha never
  once says no to anyone in this issue. The all-powerful thing has no face, no voice, and no
  fight in it, so the climax has no opponent.

### Things I was expected to already know
- The water wars (page 42). First mention, one memory panel, never detailed. Who fought?
  Over what, exactly, beyond "water"? The event the whole world is built on gets one panel.
- What Alpha actually *is*. Fifty-four pages and I cannot tell you. An AI, a government, a
  person, a policy? It tracks, restricts, authorizes, executes — and is never once defined.
- "Convenor," "handoff," "safeguards" (page 49). The vocabulary arrives all at once, late,
  in a speech.
- Mara Doss, Frank Reed, Elias Renn (page 52). Three brand-new people walk in on page 52 of
  54 and run the resolution. Who are these people?

### Lines I read twice
- "I thought she had disappeared. I stopped asking whether that meant dead or unwilling"
  (page 38). Read twice — in the good way.
- "It was the part of the protection I could still perform" (page 41).
- "The Covenant failed when fear made promises smaller than survival" (page 42). Sounds
  carved on a monument. I had to unpack it.
- "I want the decision to know who it can hurt" (page 43).
- "He carried it for fifteen years" / "Carrying is not honoring" (page 44). Who is "he"?
  Adrian? Bi11bot? And the second line is pure fortune cookie.
- "Then the system will be wrong through you" (page 49).
- "I don't trust any structure that needs that much trust in one person" (page 50). Got it,
  agree with it, noticed I was being taught it.
- "Just one that can't pretend it's clean" (page 53).

### Who I could tell apart, and who I couldn't
- Ada finally becomes her own person — the door scene is hers and it's the best her
  character ever gets.
- Leona and Mera are distinguishable as roles (mother vs. functionary) but speak in the
  exact same measured cadence. Cover the names on pages 41–43 and you can't always tell
  who's talking.
- The three representatives are interchangeable except Mara's one good question.
- Bi11bot remains the most distinct voice in the book, which says something, because he's
  the robot.

### I felt something
- Page 40, panel 3: "You chose safety for me." / "Yes." / "You chose it instead of me."
  That's the emotional peak of the whole book for me.
- Page 45, panel 2: "I'd like permission to keep trying." / "You can keep trying."
  Restrained and honest. No hug, no fix. Good.
- Page 48: grief and anger at once — he spent his last minutes on a message instead of a
  door. The book half-knows it was a selfish choice (page 49: "He also made the choice to
  leave you the burden") and half-excuses it, and I side with the half that doesn't.
- Page 54: grandmother's hands finally empty, "Mine now."

### I predicted
- Leona was the deciding vote. "I made the deciding choice" was visibly coming from the
  moment the two-of-three rule was stated.
- Alex would refuse the power. The book has never once let him take the easy win, so the
  refusal was right and completely unsurprising.
- Mera's band would stay dark.

### What I think this book is about, in one sentence
Whether anyone should hold unchecked power — Alex's answer is "not even me," and then the
book turns to me and asks the question out loud.

### Where I would have put it down
Page 52. Three strangers arrive to chair the ending and I felt the book hand itself over to
a meeting. I finished because there were two pages left, not because I was pulled.

### The last page: do I need the next issue, and why
No. The ending is honest — debt remains, scarcity remains, nothing is magically fixed — and
I respect that more than a clean victory. But the FINAL HUMAN QUESTION caption ("Can people
accept responsibility for a future no system can guarantee?") is the moment the book admits
it's a lesson. That's a discussion prompt, not an ending. The story is closed, there's no
person I'm following forward, and the last page told me to write an essay about it. I
wouldn't buy the next book because this one told me it was finished and then assigned me
homework.

VERDICT Issue 03: put down: page 52; next issue: no

## Whole book

### The page that would have lost my whole class
Page 11. It's the first page where the book stops showing and starts lecturing, and it comes
right after the best stretch in the book (pages 6–10), so it wastes the exact moment it had
us. Thirty kids, thirty phones. The ones who survived page 11 would be picked off by the
fragment parade (pages 23–26) and the meeting ending (pages 51–53), but page 11 is where
the class as a class checks out.

And one thing the class would say out loud, because they're openly suspicious of anything
that smells machine-made: this book's dialogue sounds generated. "Thinking about it isn't
doing it." "Carrying is not honoring." "Scale is not a promise." "Quiet isn't the same as
safe." Every character — miner, scientist, director, grandmother, robot — speaks in the
same polished, balanced, quote-card antithesis, and the names (Alex Phantum, Mera Vale,
Bi11bot with two 1s) have that same too-smooth ring. Nobody in this book talks like a
person. A classroom of seventeen-year-olds would clock that in the first ten pages and
never fully trust the book again.

### What I would tell a friend it was about
"A kid in a poor mining city inherits his dad's giant debt on his seventeenth birthday,
finds his dad's hidden robot, and proves the rich cities are lying about water — and then
instead of taking over the system, he makes it hold public meetings. It's less fun than
that sounds, because everyone talks in proverbs and the big showdown is a hearing. The mom
scene and the dad's death are genuinely good, though."

### One-sentence aftertaste of each issue
- Issue 01: A killer first two pages — the birthday debt inheritance — that stalls in a
  tool museum and ends on a flood I never believed.
- Issue 02: A fetch-quest tour of four wise mentors who all talk in the same quotable
  one-liners, saved by a scrap-metal fix and one creepy reflection.
- Issue 03: The mother at the door and the father's death are the real thing, but the
  climax is a meeting the all-powerful system doesn't resist, and the last page hands me
  an essay question.
